mappings.note: MISFILED: source tag 10SCIENCE5qa -- this is NCERT ch.5 Periodic Classification, not Life Processes. Content tested is whether Dobereiner triads survive inside Newlands' octaves, i.e. early classification of elements. C 1.1 is the only competency in this frame about classification of elements; CG 1 has no learning outcomes, so the competency is the finest code available.

Limitations of Dobereiner's triads -- a critique of an early classification scheme, so C 1.1 (classification of elements). Not C 1.2 (separation techniques) or C 1.3 (chemical equations): nothing is separated or reacted here.
Limitations of Newlands' Law of Octaves -- same classification competency as its Dobereiner twin. No finer code exists because CG 1 carries no LOs in this chapter's frame.

Predicting oxide formulae for K, C, Al, Si, Ba from Mendeleev's table is valency-from-position reasoning, which C 1.1 names explicitly ('properties (valency)'). Not C 1.3: no equation is balanced and no reaction is described, only a formula deduced.

Which elements later filled Mendeleev's gaps (Sc, Ge beside Ga) -- tests the predictive power of the periodic arrangement, hence C 1.1 rather than any CG 6/CG 7 history-of-science code, which concern Indian contributions and current frontiers respectively.
Mendeleev's criteria for building his table -- the organising principle of the classification itself, C 1.1.
Why noble gases get their own group -- reasoning from filled valence shells to group placement, which is C 1.1's atomic-structure-to-position link.
How the Modern table removed Mendeleev's anomalies (atomic number vs atomic mass) -- a comparison of two classifications, C 1.1.
Naming two elements chemically like magnesium and justifying it -- group membership deduced from valence-shell configuration, C 1.1.
Listing elements with one, two or filled outermost shells -- pure configuration-to-group mapping, C 1.1.

Asks what Li/Na/K atoms have in common and what He/Ne atoms have in common. The answer is valence-shell configuration, so C 1.1; the reaction with water is only the framing, not what is being assessed, which is why C 1.3 is not cited.
Which of the first ten elements are metals -- metallic character read off position in the Modern table, C 1.1.
Maximum metallic character judged from periodic-table position -- a periodicity trend, C 1.1.
Which statement about left-to-right trends is wrong -- four periodicity trends at once (metallic character, valence electrons, ionisation, oxide acidity), all inside C 1.1.
XCl2 with high melting point places X in magnesium's group -- valency-to-group inference, C 1.1. Only the group is asked for, so C 1.3 (bonding/equations) is not cited.
Five identify-the-element clues, every one phrased as a shell/valence-electron count. Configuration-to-identity is C 1.1.
What all elements in boron's column, and in fluorine's column, share -- the defining property of a group, C 1.1.
From configuration 2,8,7 give the atomic number and the chemically similar element -- configuration to position to chemical similarity, C 1.1.
Metal/non-metal, reactivity, size and ion type for three elements in groups 16-17 -- four periodicity trends, all C 1.1.
Configurations of N and P and which is more electronegative -- a down-the-group electronegativity trend, C 1.1.
How electronic configuration determines position in the Modern table -- this is the core statement of C 1.1 and nothing finer exists in the frame.
Which of Ca's neighbours (Z = 12, 19, 21, 38) resemble it -- group membership vs mere adjacency, C 1.1.
Compare and contrast Mendeleev's and the Modern table -- two classification schemes side by side, C 1.1.
Law of Octaves held only up to calcium -- a limitation of an early classification, C 1.1.
Mendeleev ordered by increasing atomic mass -- the statement of his periodic law, C 1.1.
Germanium found a place later -- the gap-filling property of Mendeleev's table, C 1.1.
Which statements about the Modern table are incorrect (ordering principle, isotope placement) -- classification rules, C 1.1.
18 vertical columns are groups, 7 horizontal rows are periods -- the structure of the Modern table, C 1.1.
Which of Z = 2, 3, 7, 10, 30 share a period -- shell count from configuration, C 1.1.

Which of Z = 9, 11, 17, 12, 13 share a group -- valence-electron count from configuration, C 1.1. Companion to the period question above, and deliberately the same code because the frame offers no group-vs-period distinction.
Where configuration 2,8 sits (group 18) -- filled shell to noble-gas group, C 1.1.
The element in every organic compound belongs to group 14 -- carbon located by group, C 1.1, which explicitly covers carbon compounds.
Outermost shell of period-2 elements is the L shell -- period number equals shell count, C 1.1.
Which of Na, Al, Si, P has most valence electrons -- group number to valence electrons, C 1.1.
Increasing atomic radii of O, F, N -- across-period size trend, C 1.1.
Largest atomic radius among Na, Mg, K -- combines the down-group and across-period size trends, C 1.1.
Which element loses an electron most easily -- electropositivity trend, C 1.1.
Which element does not lose an electron easily (F) -- the same electropositivity trend read in reverse, C 1.1.

Characteristics of isotopes, and why they share one slot -- isotopes are a classification problem for the periodic table, so C 1.1 rather than any nuclear/atomic-structure code, which this frame does not carry separately.
Order Na, Si, Cl, Mg, Al by decreasing metallic character -- across-period metallic trend, C 1.1.
Order Li, O, C, Be, F by increasing non-metallic character -- the complement of the metallic trend, C 1.1.
Eka-aluminium forms E2O3 -- oxide formula predicted from the group's valency of 3, C 1.1. Not C 1.3: the formula follows from position, no reaction is written.
B, Si and Ge are metalloids -- the metal/non-metal borderline of the table, C 1.1.

Which element forms an acidic oxide, given only atomic numbers. Two steps: locate the element and judge it a non-metal (C 1.1), then predict the acidic character of its oxide (C 1.3, which covers acid/base and metal/non-metal behaviour). Both cited because either alone leaves half the question unaccounted for.
Z = 14 is hard, has an acidic oxide and a covalent halide -- classify it. Position and metalloid classification is C 1.1; the acidic-oxide and covalent-halide evidence is C 1.3.

Which diagram represents atomic radius correctly. Figure-dependent, but the stored model answer shows the discrimination is about where the radius is measured from in a shell diagram, so the assessed idea is atomic radius as a periodic property -- C 1.1.
Which property does not increase down a group (valence) -- distinguishes valence, which is constant in a group, from radius, metallic character and shell count, which rise. C 1.1.
Atomic size decreases across a period -- the across-period size trend on its own, C 1.1.
Which set is in increasing metallic character (Be, Mg, Ca) -- down-group metallic trend, C 1.1.
Three elements whose middle atomic mass is the average of the other two -- name the arrangement (Dobereiner triad) and give an example. Early classification, C 1.1.
F to K in mass order: pick two sets of similar elements and name the law (Newlands' octaves). Early classification, C 1.1.
Testing two candidate sets against the triad rule -- applying, not just recalling, Dobereiner's criterion. Still C 1.1, the only classification competency.
Why cobalt (58.93) precedes nickel (58.71) in Mendeleev's table -- the atomic-mass anomaly that motivated atomic-number ordering, C 1.1.
Hydrogen's unique position -- it fits both group 1 and group 17 on configuration grounds, which is a C 1.1 placement argument.
Chloride formulae of Eka-silicon and Eka-aluminium -- valency predicted from group, C 1.1. Paired with qid:85505 (their oxides) and given the same code deliberately.
Group number and valency for elements with 3, 4 and 2 outermost electrons -- valence electrons to group to valency, C 1.1.

Formula AND nature of bonding of a group-14 chloride. The formula comes from valency (C 1.1); judging the bond covalent is chemical-interaction reasoning (C 1.3). Cited together because the second half is not a classification question.
Compare the radius of a 12p/12e atom with a 12p/10e cation -- effective nuclear charge and ionic vs atomic radius, still the atomic-size strand of C 1.1.

The element list is missing from the printed stem, but the stored model answer shows both parts (a second-period set and a halogen set) test the across-period and down-group radius trends. Determinable without the list, so mapped: C 1.1.
Identify which of four configurations are metals -- valence electrons to metallic character, C 1.1.
